why_here: It follows the snowshoe hare, which lives across the spruce forests of Canada and Alaska.
fun_fact: Its numbers rise and crash on a roughly ten-year cycle that tracks the hares it eats.
clue: Its huge furry paws work like snowshoes, and it lives mostly on one kind of hare.

why_here: Tens of millions once grazed the grasslands of the Great Plains, from Alberta down to Texas.
fun_fact: It is the national mammal of the United States and can run at about 55 km/h.
clue: The heaviest land animal of its home range, it rolls in dust baths called wallows.

why_here: It needs short grass where it can see predators coming, so it digs its towns across the dry western plains.
fun_fact: One colony in Texas was said to cover about 65,000 square kilometres and hold millions of animals.
clue: This chubby squirrel lives in burrow 'towns' and greets family with a kiss.

names: Gulf of St. Lawrence lowland forests

why_here: It thrives in the cold winters and rich soils of the Great Lakes, New England and the St. Lawrence valley.
fun_fact: It takes about 40 litres of sap to boil down to one litre of syrup.
clue: Its sap becomes pancake syrup, and its leaf is on a famous red and white flag.

place: The Gulf and southern Atlantic coastal plain
why_here: It needs warm, slow fresh water, which the swamps and rivers of the southeastern coastal plain have plenty of.
fun_fact: The temperature of the nest decides whether the eggs hatch as males or females.
clue: Its snout is broad and U-shaped, and it can go through thousands of teeth in a lifetime.

place: The Chihuahuan, Sonoran and Mojave deserts
why_here: It hunts lizards, snakes and insects across the hot, dry scrublands of the US Southwest and northern Mexico.
fun_fact: It can run at about 30 km/h and will kill and eat rattlesnakes.
clue: A ground-running cuckoo that a cartoon made famous for saying 'beep beep'.

why_here: It grows on the sandy, fire-swept coastal plain from Virginia to Florida and the Gulf.
fun_fact: Young trees spend years in a 'grass stage' that looks like a tuft of grass and survives fire.
clue: Frequent fires help this tree, and it once covered about 360,000 square kilometres.

why_here: It digs its burrows in the deep sandy soils under the longleaf pines of the Southeast.
fun_fact: Its burrows give shelter to more than 350 other kinds of animals.
clue: Its burrow can be 3 m deep and 12 m long, and hundreds of species move in.

why_here: It spends most of its life underground in the Sonoran Desert, coming out mainly after spring and summer rains.
fun_fact: A compound from its saliva led to a diabetes drug called exenatide.
clue: A slow, beaded orange and black lizard with a venomous bite and a fat tail.

why_here: It survives the Mojave's heat by spending most of the year in burrows.
fun_fact: It can store water in its bladder and go a year or more without drinking.
clue: It can live 50 years or more and spends up to 95% of its life underground.

why_here: It eats almost nothing but sagebrush in winter, so it lives where the sagebrush sea grows.
fun_fact: Males puff up two yellow air sacs on their chests that pop loudly when they display.
clue: In spring, males strut on dancing grounds called leks, popping air sacs on their chests.

place: California's Central Valley and oak foothills
why_here: It lives only in California, in the oak savannas and farmland of the Central Valley and nearby hills.
fun_fact: It is one of very few bird species found only in California.
clue: A long-tailed black and white crow relative with a bright yellow bill.

place: The mountains of Alaska and the Yukon
why_here: It lives on steep alpine slopes in the mountains of Alaska, the Yukon and the Mackenzie Mountains.
fun_fact: Rams' curled horns grow a ring each year, so you can count their age.
clue: This all-white wild sheep has amber curled horns and climbs steep cliffs to escape wolves.

why_here: It is the signature plant of the Chihuahuan Desert, so common that its range is used to map that desert.
fun_fact: Its tough leaf fibre, called ixtle, has long been used for brushes and rope.
clue: Its stiff, spiky leaves can puncture tyres and boots, and its fibre makes brushes.

why_here: It forms the pinyon-juniper woodlands that cover the mesas of the Colorado Plateau.
fun_fact: Pinyon jays bury its seeds by the thousands and forget some, planting new trees.
clue: Its tasty nuts were a key food for many Native peoples and are still gathered in autumn.

why_here: This small elk evolved in the grasslands and tule marshes of California's Central Valley.
fun_fact: It fell to perhaps a handful of animals in the 1870s and has recovered to several thousand.
clue: The smallest elk of its kind, named after a marsh plant, it once nearly vanished.

why_here: It nests only in the oak and Ashe juniper woods of central Texas, using juniper bark for its nest.
fun_fact: It is the only bird that breeds only in Texas.
clue: This little songbird builds its nest from strips of juniper bark and nests in one state.

why_here: It is adapted to the tall coastal grasslands along the Gulf coast of Texas and Louisiana.
fun_fact: Only a small wild flock survives, kept going by captive breeding and releases.
clue: Males inflate orange neck sacs and boom at dawn to win mates.

why_here: It rings the Central Valley in the dry foothills of California's Coast Ranges and Sierra Nevada.
fun_fact: In a drought it can drop all its leaves in summer to save water.
clue: Its leaves have a bluish tint, and it can drop them in summer to survive drought.

why_here: It grows only in the wet mountains of southwest Oregon and northwest California.
fun_fact: Its fragrant wood was so prized in Japan that logs were shipped there for temples and coffins.
clue: Garden forms of this tree, called Lawson cypress, are planted all over the world.

why_here: It grows almost only in the Vizcaíno region of central Baja California.
fun_fact: It was named after a creature in Lewis Carroll's poem 'The Hunting of the Snark'.
clue: It looks like an upside-down carrot and is named after a creature in a Lewis Carroll poem.

why_here: It lives only in cold, clear, rocky streams of the Ozarks in Missouri and Arkansas.
fun_fact: It breathes mostly through the wrinkly folds of skin along its sides.
clue: A giant salamander up to 60 cm long, nicknamed the 'snot otter'.

why_here: It lives only in the coastal sage scrub of southern California and northern Baja California.
fun_fact: Its call sounds like a kitten's mew.
clue: This tiny grey songbird mews like a kitten and depends on coastal sage scrub.

why_here: It lives in the deep loess soils of the Palouse hills of eastern Washington and Idaho.
fun_fact: It was long rumoured to smell like lilies, but recent finds did not back that up.
clue: This rare pale worm can be close to a metre long and was once thought lost.

why_here: It grows in the bare, wind-carved 'blowouts' of the Nebraska Sand Hills.
fun_fact: It was once thought to be one of the rarest plants on the Great Plains.
clue: Its pale blue flowers smell of vanilla, and it grows in bowls blown out by wind.

why_here: Its caterpillars feed on Kincaid's lupine, which grows in the Willamette Valley's remnant grasslands.
fun_fact: It was thought extinct for over 50 years until it was found again in 1989.
clue: This small blue butterfly was lost for decades and depends on one kind of lupine.

why_here: This black bear subspecies lives in the wet coastal forests of central and northern British Columbia.
fun_fact: In some places up to one in ten is born white thanks to a recessive gene, yet it is not an albino.
clue: A black bear that is sometimes born creamy white, and fishes for salmon in daylight.

why_here: It grows on rocky slopes across the Sonoran and Chihuahuan deserts of the US Southwest and northern Mexico.
fun_fact: It can grow a full set of leaves within days of a rain and drop them again when it dries out.
clue: Its whip-like spiny stems look dead most of the year, then leaf out days after rain.

why_here: It lives among granite rocks and snowmelt in the high Sierra Nevada of California.
fun_fact: It can curl into a ball and roll downhill to escape danger.
clue: This flat-headed salamander has webbed toes for clinging to wet granite near snowfields.
